fields.sample_size: qualitative field study in four rural districts of Tanzania (Kigoma rural, Same, Iramba, Nzega; July 2008-August 2009): interviews with district water engineers and planning officers; four wards in two districts (one historically low-investment and one high-investment ward each) with interviews and group discussions with elected representatives, village and ward officers and randomly selected villagers; 50% of Same wards visited briefly; ministry interviews and document review; number of interviews not stated
fields.effect_measure: qualitative policy and resource-allocation analysis at ministry, district and village levels; descriptive figures from programme documents (no inferential statistics)
fields.effect_estimate: The Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Program (launched 2006; targets 65% rural coverage by 2010, 74% by 2015 and 90% by 2025; estimated cost 1,606 million US dollars) allocates water funds top-down through the Local Government Capital Development Grant system (about 1.5 USD per person per year; half decided at sub-district level through village plans, half at district level with no specific allocation procedure; LGCDG funds were 32.74% of development funds transferred to districts in 2007/2008) and through development grants to qualified districts; reported coverage by district in 2005 ranged from 6.4% to 91.8%. Water funds do not feed from village plans, villages usually choose one project a year (typically classrooms, dispensaries, roads), and allocation at district level follows national directives and political influence; only a small proportion of funds reaches the underserved areas. The authors argue for a stronger link between bottom-up and top-down planning, more downward accountability and, meanwhile, more central-government intervention, grounded in the right to water (non-exclusion, non-discrimination, participation).
fields.section: Full text (13 pages): Introduction; Methodology; Decentralization in Tanzania; RWSSP; resource allocation at ministry, district and village levels; Discussion; Conclusions
fields.exact_location: Methodology (field work in four districts and four wards); Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Program section and Table 3 (responsibilities by level); allocation sections; Conclusions; Sustainability Science 6(1):37-49

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a qualitative policy analysis of the allocation of rural water funds in Tanzania, based on ministry interviews, document review and field work in four districts and four wards; read in full text 2026-10-04. Descriptive programme figures only; no effect estimate.
